festivals.name: Aboakyer
festivals.when: Usually the first weekend of May
festivals.sum: Two Asafo companies race to catch a live bushbuck with sticks and bare hands, an offering to the god Penkye Otu.

festivals.name: Addae Tuntum
festivals.when: Usually January, sometimes December
festivals.keeper: The chiefs and people of Kukuom
festivals.sum: Kukuom remembers the Ebirimoro war with the Sefwi, and renews its loyalty to its chief.

festivals.name: Adekyem
festivals.when: Every two years, usually November or December
festivals.keeper: The chiefs and people of the Bechem Traditional Area
festivals.sum: Bechem’s festival every two years: its history and culture on show, and funds raised for education and development.

festivals.name: Adikanfo
festivals.when: Usually September
festivals.keeper: The chiefs and people of Hwidiem
festivals.sum: Hwidiem remembers its migration from Denkyira Ntomu, with a durbar of chiefs, drumming and dancing.

festivals.name: Agbamevoza
festivals.when: Usually late August or early September, over a week
festivals.sum: The Kente festival of Agotime: weaving contests and chiefs in their finest cloth.

festivals.name: Akwantukese
festivals.when: November or December, over a month
festivals.sum: New Juaben remembers its great migration from Juaben in Ashanti, with a procession and durbar in Koforidua.

festivals.name: Akwasidae
festivals.when: Every six weeks, on a Sunday
festivals.sum: The Asantehene sits in state at Manhyia and receives chiefs and visitors, every six weeks.

festivals.name: Apoo
festivals.when: Usually March or April; dates vary
festivals.keeper: The Bono of Techiman and Wenchi
festivals.sum: A week when people may sing out their grievances against chiefs and leaders, to cleanse the town.
festivals.dateSetBy: The Techiman and Wenchi Traditional Councils

festivals.name: Asafotufiam
festivals.when: Late July or early August, with the durbar on a Saturday
festivals.sum: Ada’s warriors’ festival: Asafo companies re-enact old battles, with musketry and a durbar of chiefs in palanquins.

festivals.name: Asogli Te Za
festivals.when: September
festivals.sum: The yam festival of the Asogli State at Ho, honouring the hunter said to have found the first yam.

festivals.name: Bakatue
festivals.when: The first Tuesday of July, with a durbar that Saturday
festivals.sum: Elmina opens the Benya lagoon: the chief casts a net three times, then come the regatta and a durbar at the castle.

festivals.name: Buem Lilu
festivals.when: Usually the second week of October; the Buem Traditional Council sets the date
festivals.keeper: The Buem people, led by the Omanhene at Bodada
festivals.sum: The Buem yam festival: three weeks of rites in the towns, then a grand durbar at Bodada.

festivals.name: Bugum
festivals.when: The ninth day of Bugum Goli, the first lunar month (about late June in 2026)
festivals.sum: The Dagomba new-year fire festival: torches carried through the streets and out of town at night.
festivals.dateSetBy: The lunar calendar, announced by the chiefs

festivals.name: Chale Wote
festivals.when: Usually August, over about a week
festivals.sum: Accra’s street art festival: murals, performance, music and film in the streets of James Town and beyond.

festivals.name: Damba in Nalerigu
festivals.when: The lunar month of Damba (about late August in 2026); the Mamprusi calendar sets the day
festivals.sum: Mamprugu’s great gathering: chiefs from across the kingdom, dances through the night and the Nayiri at sunrise.

festivals.name: Damba
festivals.when: The month of Damba, the third lunar month (about late August in 2026)
festivals.sum: Drumming, smocks and chiefs on horseback, in the month that marks the Prophet’s birth.

festivals.name: Edina Bronya
festivals.when: Usually the first Thursday of January
festivals.sum: Elmina’s own “Christmas”, born of its Dutch years, with rites at the Benya Lagoon and chiefs in palanquins.

festivals.name: Eluo
festivals.when: Set each year by the Wiawso Traditional Council; October to mid-November in 2023
festivals.keeper: The chiefs and people of Sefwi Wiawso
festivals.sum: The Sefwi yam festival: a week of events that ends with a grand durbar of chiefs at Sefwi Wiawso.

festivals.name: Fao
festivals.when: Around the turn of the year, usually December or January
festivals.sum: Navrongo’s thanksgiving at the end of the farming season, with a durbar, drumming and war dances.

festivals.name: Fetu Afahye
festivals.when: The first week of September, peaking on the first Saturday
festivals.sum: Cape Coast’s week of cleansing and thanksgiving, with Asafo companies, state umbrellas and a grand procession.

festivals.name: Fiok
festivals.when: December (21 December in 2024)
festivals.sum: The Builsa remember their victory over the slave raider Babatu, with warriors in horned headdresses.

festivals.name: Fofie
festivals.when: October
festivals.sum: A yam festival of thanks for the harvest, ending in a durbar of chiefs carried through the streets.

festivals.name: Frikooso Afahye
festivals.when: October
festivals.place: Tapa Abotoase and the Tapa towns
festivals.keeper: The chiefs and people of the Tapa Traditional Area
festivals.sum: Tapa remembers the battle at Frikooso hill, where its people and their allies turned back an Asante army.

festivals.name: Fussikur
festivals.when: Between February and March
festivals.keeper: The chiefs and people of Bowiri
festivals.sum: Bowiri remembers its journey from Moree: a week of rites, a climb to the old settlement and a grand durbar.

festivals.name: Gidifon
festivals.when: August to September
festivals.keeper: The Adele, with their chief priests
festivals.sum: The Adele new yam festival: offerings of mashed yam on the mountain, then yam fufu and dancing at home.

festivals.name: Godigbeza
festivals.when: October or November
festivals.keeper: The chiefs and people of Aflao
festivals.sum: Aflao’s festival of liberation, remembering the escape from King Agorkoli’s rule at Notsie, with a grand durbar.

festivals.name: Gyogyi
festivals.when: Usually September (the season runs August to November)
festivals.place: The Akyode towns around Keri and Nkwanta
festivals.keeper: The Akyode, with the chief priest of the Brukum stool
festivals.sum: The Akyode yam festival: the stool blesses the new yam, chiefs swear to the chief priest, and the night is for dancing.

festivals.name: Hogbetsotso
festivals.when: Usually the first Saturday of November
festivals.sum: The Anlo remember their escape from King Agorkoli at Notsie, walking backwards to hide their tracks.

festivals.name: Homowo
festivals.when: August into September, each Ga town in turn
festivals.sum: “Hooting at hunger”: kpokpoi is shared and sprinkled for the ancestors.
festivals.dateSetBy: The Ga Traditional Council, with each Ga town setting its own days

festivals.name: Hyirebo
festivals.when: The first week of April
festivals.keeper: The chiefs and people of Bowiri Amanforo
festivals.sum: A week of peace that closes the Bowiri year: river bathing at dawn, white clay and a durbar.

festivals.name: Jintigi
festivals.when: Usually April
festivals.keeper: The chiefs and people of Gonja
festivals.sum: The Gonja fire festival: torches carried at night to the edge of town, and readings for the year ahead.

festivals.name: Kobine
festivals.when: September or October, over four days
festivals.sum: Lawra’s harvest festival, famous for its dance competition to kuor drums and ankle bells.

festivals.name: Kpledjoo
festivals.when: Usually late March or early April
festivals.sum: Tema’s festival at the Sakumo lagoon: two days of rites, processions and prayers for fish and food.

festivals.name: Krachi Yam Festival
festivals.when: September
festivals.keeper: The Krachi, led by the Krachiwura
festivals.sum: Krachi and its yam-growing neighbours give thanks for the harvest, with masquerades and yam pounded in the open.

festivals.name: Kundum
festivals.when: July to November, one town after another
festivals.place: The coast from Sekondi to Axim
festivals.sum: The harvest festival of the Ahanta and Nzema, moving from town to town along the western coast.

festivals.name: Kwafie
festivals.when: November or December
festivals.keeper: The Bono of Dormaa and their neighbours
festivals.sum: A festival of fire and of putting the town in order, ending in a grand durbar at Dormaa Ahenkro.

festivals.name: Kwahu Easter
festivals.when: Easter weekend (March or April)
festivals.keeper: Kwahu towns, with the Ghana Tourism Authority
festivals.sum: Ghana’s biggest homecoming: Easter on the Kwahu ridge, with paragliding off the Odweanoma mountain.

festivals.name: Ngmayem
festivals.when: The last week of October (25 Oct–2 Nov in 2026)
festivals.sum: The Krobo millet festival and new year, with a pilgrimage to Krobo Mountain and a grand durbar.

festivals.name: Nyigbla
festivals.when: Usually the third weekend of February
festivals.keeper: The chiefs and people of Afife
festivals.sum: A week of thanksgiving at Afife that remembers the Anlo-Ewe migration, ending in war dances and bonfires.

festivals.name: Odwira
festivals.when: September or October, over a week
festivals.sum: Akuapem’s week of purification and the new yam, remembering the 1826 victory at Katamanso.

festivals.name: Ohum
festivals.when: A Tuesday or Wednesday in June or July, and again in September or October
festivals.sum: Akyem thanksgiving for the yam harvest and the Birim river, held twice a year after two weeks of silence.

festivals.name: Ovazu
festivals.when: At the fonio harvest, October to December
festivals.sum: The Akposo thanksgiving for the fonio harvest, to God and the seven principal Akposo gods.

festivals.name: Paragbiele
festivals.when: Late January into February
festivals.keeper: The chiefs and people of Tumu
festivals.sum: Tumu’s harvest thanksgiving, with farm produce on show, a durbar of chiefs, drumming and dance.

festivals.name: Sasadu
festivals.when: October, hosted by each town in turn
festivals.sum: Four Volta towns of one origin renew their old friendship, taking turns to host a grand durbar.

festivals.name: Winneba Masquerade
festivals.when: 1 January
festivals.keeper: The Winneba Masquerade Federation and its five clubs
festivals.sum: Five masquerade clubs in masks and costumes march and dance for the prize on New Year’s Day.

festivals.name: Yaa Asantewaa Festival
festivals.when: Usually early August
festivals.sum: Ejisu honours Nana Yaa Asantewaa, the queen mother who led the 1900 war against the British.

places.name: Jamestown
places.note: Fishing harbour, boxing gyms and one of Accra's oldest quarters.

places.name: Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park
places.note: Ghana's most visited attraction: the mausoleum and museum of the first president.

places.name: Makola Market
places.note: The city's central market. Cloth, food, and most other things.

places.name: Labadi Beach
places.note: Accra's busiest stretch of sand, liveliest at the weekend.

places.name: Osu
places.note: Food, bars and late-night Accra around Oxford Street.

places.name: Arts Centre for National Culture
places.note: Carving, kente and craft stalls near the sea.

places.name: Cape Coast Castle
places.note: A UNESCO World Heritage site, and a place of difficult, necessary history.

places.name: Kakum National Park
places.note: Rainforest, and a canopy walkway strung between the trees.

places.name: Elmina Castle
places.note: Begun in 1482, the oldest European-built structure in sub-Saharan Africa.

places.name: Assin Manso Ancestral Slave River
places.note: The last bathing place before the coast, now a site of return.

places.name: Hans Cottage Botel
places.note: Crocodiles and birdlife a short drive from Cape Coast.

places.name: Wli Falls
places.note: Ghana's highest waterfall, reached on a walk through forest.

places.name: Mount Afadja
places.note: The country's highest peak. Steep, but a short climb.

places.name: Tafi Atome Monkey Sanctuary
places.note: Mona monkeys living alongside the village that protects them.

places.name: Amedzofe
places.note: One of Ghana’s highest settlements, with the Ote waterfall below it.

places.name: Keta Lagoon
places.note: Sandbars, salt and birds between the lagoon and the sea.

places.name: Mole National Park
places.note: Ghana's largest park: elephants, antelope and walking safaris.

places.name: Larabanga Mosque
places.note: Sudanese-style mud and stick architecture, among the oldest in the country.

places.name: Mognori Eco Village
places.note: Canoe safaris and village stays on the edge of Mole.

places.name: Salaga
places.note: A town carrying a heavy history as a trading and slave-market centre.

places.name: Daboya
places.note: Known for smock weaving and for salt.

places.name: Nzulezu
places.note: A village built on stilts over the Amansuri wetland, reached by canoe.

places.name: Busua Beach
places.note: Surf lessons, slow afternoons and a walkable beach town.

places.name: Cape Three Points
places.note: The southernmost point of Ghana, with a lighthouse and forest reserve.

places.name: Fort San Antonio, Axim
places.note: A Portuguese fort of 1515, above the sea.

places.name: Ankasa Conservation Area
places.note: Dense rainforest in the far southwest.

places.name: Manhyia Palace Museum
places.note: The Asantehene's former palace, now a museum of Asante history.

places.name: Kejetia Market
places.note: One of the largest markets in West Africa.

places.name: The Great Hall, KNUST
places.note: A landmark of Ghanaian modernist architecture.

places.name: Lake Bosomtwe
places.note: A meteorite crater lake ringed by villages.

places.name: Bonwire
places.note: The kente weaving village.

places.name: Ntonso
places.note: Adinkra cloth, stamped by hand.

places.name: Aburi Botanical Gardens
places.note: Long-established gardens in cool hill air above Accra.

places.name: Akosombo Dam
places.note: The dam that made Lake Volta.

places.name: Boti Falls
places.note: Twin falls, fullest in the rainy season.

places.name: Umbrella Rock
places.note: A mushroom-shaped rock formation on the walk near Boti.

places.name: Bunso Arboretum
places.note: Forest, birds and a canopy walkway.

places.name: Central Mosque, Tamale
places.note: The landmark at the centre of the city.

places.name: Tamale Central Market
places.note: Smocks, shea butter and northern produce.

places.name: Gbewaa Palace, Yendi
places.note: The seat of the Dagbon kingdom.

places.name: Paga Crocodile Pond
places.note: Crocodiles that live alongside the community around them.

places.name: Bolgatanga Market
places.note: The home of the Bolga basket.

places.name: Sirigu
places.note: Painted compound walls, and a women’s pottery and art collective.

places.name: Tongo Hills and Tengzug
places.note: Rock formations and a long-standing shrine.

places.name: Navrongo Cathedral
places.note: An earth-built cathedral with painted interior walls.

places.name: Wa Naa's Palace
places.note: Sudanese-style earth architecture in the regional capital.

places.name: Wechiau Community Hippo Sanctuary
places.note: Hippos on the Black Volta, run by the communities along it.

places.name: Gwollu Defence Wall
places.note: A wall built to resist slave raiders.

places.name: Nandom
places.note: Known for its cathedral and its harvest festival.

places.name: Nalerigu
places.note: The regional capital, with old earth-built architecture.

places.name: Naa Jaringa Wall, Gambaga
places.note: What survives of the defensive wall around old Gambaga.

places.name: Gambaga Escarpment
places.note: A long ridge with views out over the plains.

places.name: Nakpanduri
places.note: Escarpment views at the eastern edge of the region.

places.name: Lake Volta at Dambai
places.note: The ferry crossing, and the working life of the lake.

places.name: Kyabobo National Park
places.note: Hills, forest and wildlife near the Togo border.

places.name: Nkwanta
places.note: A base for walking in the Kyabobo hills.

places.name: Sunyani
places.note: A green regional capital with a steady pace.

places.name: Bui National Park
places.note: Forest, the Black Volta and hippos.

places.name: Kintampo Waterfalls
places.note: Steps down through forest to the falls.

places.name: Techiman Market
places.note: One of the biggest produce markets in the country.

places.name: Fuller Falls
places.note: A quieter waterfall near Kintampo.

places.name: Buoyem Caves
places.note: Bat caves and rock formations.

places.name: Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary
places.note: Mona and colobus monkeys protected by the villages around them.

places.name: Goaso
places.note: The regional capital, in the middle of cocoa country.

places.name: Mim
places.note: A timber and cocoa town.

places.name: Kenyasi
places.note: A growing town in the Asutifi district.

places.name: Bia National Park
places.note: Forest reserve and national park in the far west.

places.name: Sefwi Wiawso
places.note: The regional capital, above the cocoa country.

places.name: Cocoa country
places.note: Some of Ghana's most productive cocoa farmland.
